prompt:
Wearable ECG recordings during exercise are corrupted by motion artefact
that overlaps the heartbeat's frequency band, so band-pass filtering
removes signal with the noise. Adaptive filtering with an accelerometer
reference helps only partially. Want a different approach to separating
the cardiac signal from the motion artefact.

Incorporate ideas from Economic, Social, and Public Health Issues in Russia and Globally (Social Sciences > Decision Sciences > Management Science and Operations Research > Economic, Social, and Public Health Issues in Russia and Globally) into your approach.
proposal:
A quick flag before the technical content: that category — "Economic, Social, and Public Health Issues in Russia and Globally," filed under Decision Sciences/Management Science — is a macro-level economics and public-health-policy classification. It has no methodological or empirical bearing on separating cardiac signal from motion artifact in a wearable ECG trace; there's no genuine bridge between national public-health economics and single-channel biosignal denoising. I'm not going to manufacture a tortured link just to check that box — it would dilute the answer with filler. If you meant to attach a different reference category (e.g., something in signal processing, biomedical engineering, or statistics), let me know and I'll fold it in properly. Here's the substance instead.

## Why the current approach is stuck

- **Band-pass filtering** assumes artifact and cardiac signal live in disjoint frequency bands. During exercise they don't — footstrike/limb-swing energy smears into 0.5–40 Hz, directly overlapping QRS and even P/T-wave content. Any cutoff aggressive enough to kill the artifact also flattens the signal you want.
- **Adaptive filtering with an accelerometer reference** (LMS/NLMS/RLS) assumes the artifact is a *linear, time-invariant function* of the accelerometer signal. In reality the coupling from limb motion → electrode-skin interface → recorded voltage is nonlinear, lag-varying, and depends on electrode contact pressure, sweat, skin stretch — things the accelerometer doesn't fully capture. That's why it only partially works: it removes the *linearly correlated* component and leaves a nonlinear residual that still swamps the ECG.

The fix isn't a better filter in the same family — it's reframing the problem from **filtering** (remove a frequency band or a linearly-correlated component) to **source separation / model-based reconstruction** (recover a known-shape signal from a mixture using structure the artifact doesn't share).

## Approaches worth pursuing, roughly in order of practicality

**1. Gate before you filter — don't process uniformly.**
Most of the record is clean; the artifact is bursty (impact events, not continuous). Compute a per-segment signal quality index (kurtosis, spectral flatness of the ECG channel, accelerometer energy/jerk) and only intervene in flagged windows. This alone fixes the core complaint — blanket band-pass filtering damages *clean* segments too. Everywhere else, pass the raw signal through untouched.

**2. Model-based reconstruction (nonlinear Kalman/particle filter) inside flagged windows.**
Use a dynamical ECG model (McSharry's ECGSYN-style state-space model, or a patient-specific template built from clean beats) as the process model, and run an Extended/Unscented Kalman filter or particle filter with the corrupted samples as noisy observations. Because the model constrains the waveform shape (PQRST morphology), it can reconstruct through in-band artifact that a linear filter can't distinguish from signal. This is the standard approach in the ECG-denoising literature for motion-corrupted ambulatory recordings and tends to outperform Wiener/adaptive filtering specifically in the overlapping-band case.

**3. Morphological/sparse component separation (dictionary learning).**
Learn two dictionaries via K-SVD or similar — one on clean QRS-complex morphology, one on artifact bursts (which look impulsive/broadband, not periodic-at-heart-rate). Morphological Component Analysis then decomposes the mixture by exploiting that each source is sparse in a *different* basis, rather than in a different frequency band. This handles the "artifact and signal overlap spectrally" problem directly, since separability comes from shape/sparsity structure, not spectral content.

**4. Multichannel spatial separation, if you have >1 electrode or can add one.**
Cardiac dipole projection and motion-artifact injection have different spatial signatures across electrode pairs. Even two ECG leads plus ICA (or a simple spatial filter trained on artifact-free calibration data) can separate sources that are inseparable on a single channel, because motion artifact and the cardiac source are only linearly *independent*, not spectrally disjoint.

**5. Learned, accelerometer-conditioned denoising (if you have training data).**
Train a 1D convolutional/U-Net denoising autoencoder on ECG segments with real motion artifact overlaid (collect paired clean/corrupted data from a treadmill protocol, or synthetically inject real recorded artifact bursts onto clean rest-ECG). Feed the accelerometer/gyroscope trace in as a conditioning channel rather than as a linear regressor — let the network learn the nonlinear coupling that NLMS/RLS can't. This generalizes (2) and (3) but needs a real training set; worth it only if you're already instrumenting subjects for reference-grade concurrent ECG.

## Practical recommendation

Combine **(1) gating** with **(2) model-based reconstruction** first — it's the best effort-to-payoff ratio, doesn't need a training corpus, and directly targets your stated failure mode (broadband, in-band, bursty artifact) instead of assuming linear separability. Add multichannel spatial separation (4) if your hardware allows a second lead — that's usually the single biggest lever, since it turns an underdetermined single-channel problem into a well-posed source-separation one.
